title: What If You Were the Last Human on Earth?
analysis_notes: Downloaded on the Spark at 854x480 30fps (format 397 + opus 251, 25 MB, kept since <300 MB) to ~/studio/refs/whatif/J3XahLkDEzU.mp4 with info.json, webp thumbnail and en/en-orig auto-subs (word-timed, 1,598 words). Metadata at about 09:25 UTC: 914,113 views, 4,087 likes (0.45% like rate, low; viewers watch passively), 616 comments, 19k subs, posted 2026-10-13 (about 3 weeks old). YouTube chapters: 0:00 The first day alone, 1:00 The grid goes dark, 2:02 Living off the leftovers, 3:23 Adapting to the new world, 4:50 Marking the passage of time, 6:06 The first year's challenges, 7:28 Years of solitude, 9:27 Decades of silence and hope. Category Film & Animation; 20 SEO tags ('last human on earth', 'what if everyone disappeared', 'life after humans', 'nature reclaims earth', '20 years alone'...). Frames sampled every 2 s (330) -> contact sheet sheets/J3XahLkDEzU.jpg (15x22 grid; frame n = t 2n s, row-major); scene detection (ffmpeg scene>0.25) found 149 cuts. Full timestamped transcript at research/library/transcripts/J3XahLkDEzU.txt. Style: a single recurring cartoon protagonist (bulging round eyes, spiky hair, brass goggles, teal jacket) in flat-shaded 2.5D/low-poly city sets with ink outlines and a muted, desaturated palette, alternating with very minimal cream-paper infographics (thin lines, one teal or red accent). British-English narrator ('petrol', 'tins', 'allotments', 'lift'), calm, dry and witty, in second person. Audio mean -18 dB, peak -0.7 dB; quiet music bed with about 8 music-only holds (4-15 s) at emotional peaks. It is a 'documentary story' rather than a list: one character, one timeline (Day 1 -> Year 20), real science facts as the problems in a survival story, and a fiction twist at the end. Don't reuse its story, jokes, character design or wording.
title_pattern: 'What If You Were the Last Human on Earth?' = [What If] + [You] + [extreme, total, simple scenario]. Second person ('You') makes the viewer the subject; 'Last Human on Earth' is a well-known high-search phrase (tags repeat its variants). Under 45 characters, no number, no clickbait adjectives. The thumbnail adds what the title leaves out (the time span Day 1 -> Year 20), so title and thumbnail do different jobs. Reusable: 'What If You Were the Only Person Awake?', 'What If You Lived Alone on the Moon for 20 Years?'.

thumbnail.source: Custom 1280x720 thumbnail (not a video frame, but drawn in the same style and with the same assets as the video).
thumbnail.composition: Before/after split screen divided by a slanted white bar. Left: the grey Day 1 coffee street (stopped cars, the tallest tower centred on the vanishing point). Right: the same kind of street on Year 20, overgrown with bushes, windows broken. The hero's head and shoulders sit in the bottom corner of each half, the same pose and grin, cropped at the chest: clean-shaven on the left, grey-bearded with a missing goggles lens on the right. Each half has a yellow label in the top corner.
thumbnail.text: Two yellow road-sign style labels with black outline and heavy black sans: 'DAY 1' (left) and 'YEAR 20' (right). Only 3 words in total.
thumbnail.colours: Left half cool greys/beige with a little teal (coffee awning); right half olive and leaf greens. Saturated yellow labels and white cartoon eyes are the brightest values. Overall muted, so the yellow tags and the eyes pop.
thumbnail.subject_scale_contrast: The face is huge (about 45% of frame height per half) against a deep perspective street, so you see a person and a whole world at once. The grin is the same in both halves, but the beard, the lost lens and the weeds show 20 years passing. That is the whole video in one image.
thumbnail.why_it_works: The before/after split is easy to read at mobile size and asks 'what happened in between?'. The same face makes it a story about a person, not a lecture. The cheerful expression in a post-apocalyptic setting is unexpected (curiosity, not doom). Day/Year labels promise a timeline structure, the binge-able 'Day 1 to Year N' format.

hook.verbatim_0_to_5s: You're fourth in the queue for coffee, then you're first, then there's no queue, no barista.
hook.verbatim_5_to_28s: Four coffees still steaming and a card machine beeping approved at nobody. Outside, the street has emptied mid-sentence. Cars stopped where they were, a dog lead with nobody on the end of it. Your phone still works. Nobody answers it. Your feed stops at 14 minutes past 9:00. As far as you can tell, you're the last person on Earth.
hook.device: Cold open in the middle of an ordinary moment, in second person and present tense: the disappearance is shown as a countdown ('fourth... first... no queue') instead of being explained. Then a run of specific, uncanny leftovers (steaming coffees, 'approved at nobody', a dog lead with nobody on it, a feed frozen at 9:14), each a small 'show, don't tell' image. The premise sentence is held back to 28 s and spoken quietly, as a conclusion the viewer has already reached. No title, no channel intro, no 'in this video'. The hook also plants the dog, the billboard and the crossroads, which come back as callbacks at 4:14, 6:45 and 9:42.
hook.visual: First frame: a warm, readable cafe interior with the hero from behind in the queue. People vanish between cuts at 2.9 s and 4 s; inserts every ~2 s (cups, card machine, face).

beats.summary: No intro. 'You're fourth in the queue for coffee, then you're first, then there's no queue' — the vanishing told as a countdown of the queue, then uncanny leftovers: four coffees still steaming, a card machine beeping 'approved' at nobody.

Street emptied mid-sentence, cars stopped, a dog lead with nobody on the end of it, phone works but nobody answers, feed stops at 9:14. Then the premise line: 'you're the last person on Earth.' Plants the dog and the 'We're always here' billboard for later callbacks.
Split-flap 'DAY 1 / The Queue' sign over the river-and-skyline establishing shot, music sting.

Upside first: you stop paying, breakfast is every pastry, the car you wanted since you were nine, the penthouse on floor 41. The city runs on autopilot 'for nobody' (driverless trains, traffic lights): a repeated phrase that sets up the turn.

'It can't keep that up.' The grid explained as a balancing act (seesaw diagram), the 2003 North America blackout (500+ generators in ~7 min) as a dot-map stat, expert estimate 'hours, maybe a day'; reactors shut themselves down, 'designed for nobody'.
At 8:10 pm the penthouse goes dark, then the street, then the city district by district. Slow, near-silent visual beat.
'And you see what the lights were hiding': the Milky Way. 1994 Los Angeles earthquake blackout anecdote (people phoned the observatory about a silver cloud). A reward after the loss.
'DAY 5 / The Top Floor'.

The tap coughs: water arrives by gravity but no longer climbs (diagram of reservoir and tower, building cross-section draining). Then the smell: freezers last ~2 days, these have had five. Comic disgust face.
Down 41 floors with everything you own; 'You lose a lens on floor 19' (a goggles lens falls off, a running visual gag that stays for the rest of the film).

'An inheritance with a countdown': an expiry timeline that grows bar by bar (fresh food days, petrol months, tinned fruit ~1.5 years, pills years, beans and rice decades). Thesis: calories aren't the problem, vitamins might be, the grid stuff already is. Plants the saved tin of peaches 'for a special occasion' (pays off in the last shot).
Leaves the supermarket to 'go looking for somewhere a person could actually live'. 'DAY 50 / The Lock House'.

A lockkeeper's cottage chosen the way people have chosen homes for 10,000 years (water, soil, nothing taller than you; flat diagram). 200 allotment sheds of tools and seeds. The best vehicle is a cargo bike.
Pharmacy raid, then 'your gums have started to bleed': scurvy, the sailors' disease; 7 weeks of pastries and tins will do it. Plant potatoes. Small, physical, believable stakes.
'The nights are the hardest part. Not the dark, the quiet.' First mention of loneliness.

The dog from the coffee shop (from the 16 s shot) is in a shed with puppies. Science: which pet dogs survive; the 14-week socialisation window (bar graphic). One puppy follows you home. Delayed naming joke: 'after the thing she likes most about you' = a TINS bowl.
'DAY 100 / Lost Count' (overlaps end of previous beat).

'It's day 100, probably.' Tally marks on brick. Michel Siffre 1962 cave anecdote (thought it was 20 Aug, it was mid-September; calendar flip cards). Fix: mark sunrise against the skyline until it stops: midsummer, 21 June. 'You were 9 days out.'

Solar panels all switched off on day one by design (anti-islanding: cut out within 2 s to protect engineers; 'there are no engineers'). Rewire the cottage to camper-van batteries: '11 days and two small fires'. Then one bulb: 'the first light in the city you made yourself', held on a ~14 s music-only shot.
Split-flap flips DAY -> 'YEAR 1 / First Winter'.
The city freezes; split pipes flood floors, 'that's how buildings start to die'. German cockroach dies without central heating: 'So much for inheriting the earth.'

'Some nights you nearly don't either. Not from the cold, from the quiet.' Alexander Selkirk anecdote (worst months the first eight, tamed cats, sang and danced). You talk to the man on the bank advert (callback to the 12 s billboard): 'He's a good listener.'
Something crosses the night sky in pieces: the ISS re-entering because nobody boosted it. 'For 25 years there was always somebody up there. Now there's nobody up there either.'
You bake a cake, Tins eats most of it, peaches tin still on the sill. 'It's spring. You're still here.' Long music hold.

Corner year counter ticks Year 2..9 with one fact and one joke per year: bus-shelter greenhouse; water wheel plus car alternator (tens of watts); chickens need a rooster, 'so now you have an alarm clock'; apple grafting, a pip gives 'a random apple'; 'Year seven, you pull out your own tooth. You don't talk about year seven.'

The city has turned green: water does most of the damage (house cross-section), concrete towers stand a century. Chernobyl wolves 7x more common than in reserves; you hear them across the water. Tins is getting old, still never catches a deer. The big project: a solar radio station on the water tower.
Earth's radio bubble (~80 ly out, mostly too faint past ~16 ly, radar the loudest), and inside it a growing 'shell of silence' nearly 10 ly thick since everyone vanished. Concentric-ring diagram.
Every evening you add one small voice: Morse, 'CQ. Calling anyone.' Music hold; then 'YEAR 20 / Still Here' card (weathered, overgrown sign).

Reading glasses (the city left about a million pairs). Tins is under the apple tree; her granddaughter sleeps on your boots, also called Tins ('never good with names'). Callbacks: the coffee crossroads is a birch wood; the stadium is full again with horses (Chernobyl's 36 horses -> 130+). The last lights not yours are tritium exit signs, halving every 12 years.
'Every tooth and every cut is a gamble now.' You still climb the tower every evening: 'CQ, still here.' Zoom out to a dark Earth with one light.
'Everything up to now scientists more or less agree on. This next part, nobody can tell you.' Signals the switch from science to fiction and keeps the trust earned so far.

'On day 7,135, the radio answers.' The needle moves; a light rises over the birch wood; a saucer lands in the garden. They set out when Earth was the loudest thing for light-years, came all this way to meet 8 billion people.
'They're 20 years late and they've parked on the cabbages.' The hero steps out holding the saved tin of peaches: the special occasion has come.
Black, then 'ODDLY ELSEWHERE' wordmark. No subscribe ask in the narration.

pacing.words_per_minute_while_speaking: about 160-165 (about 70 s of music-only holds removed)
pacing.music_only_holds: about 8 holds of 4-15 s at 0:28 (title), 1:51-2:02 (Milky Way), 4:37-4:50 (naming the puppy), 5:51-6:06 (first bulb), 7:13-7:28 (Day 365 cake), 9:13-9:27 (CQ), 10:11-10:22 (CQ still here), 10:33-10:38 (radio answers)
pacing.shot_length_range: 1-3 s during the hook and the montages; 10-30 s holds for infographic builds (one camera, elements animate in) and for emotional moments
pacing.chapter_cards: 7 split-flap location cards (Day 1, 5, 50, 100, Year 1, 10, 20), i.e. one roughly every 80-90 s, each a reset and progress marker
pacing.rehook_interval_s: about 20-40 s: each section opens with a new problem ('It can't keep that up', 'the tap coughs', 'your gums have started to bleed', 'you lost a week', 'every panel switched itself off') that is solved within 30-60 s; a joke lands about every 30 s
pacing.notes: The rhythm is problem -> real science fact or historical anecdote -> practical fix -> dry joke -> small emotional beat, repeated per chapter, then sped up in the years montage (one sentence per year) and slowed down for the ending. Narration is calm and dry, never shouted. Silence is used as punctuation.

techniques_worth_copying: Day-counter spine: the scenario is one character's timeline (Day 1 -> 5 -> 50 -> 100 -> Year 1 -> 10 -> 20) shown with a physical split-flap sign over the same establishing shot. The sign and the view age with the story (clean -> snowy -> rusty with vines), so a single reused shot is the chapter card, the progress bar and the time-lapse.
Second-person, present-tense narration ('You're fourth in the queue... you bake a cake'), so the viewer lives the what-if instead of being lectured.

Science as the obstacle in the story: each fact (grid balance, gravity water, freezer life, expiry dates, scurvy, puppy socialisation, anti-islanding solar, frozen pipes, ISS orbit decay, radio bubble) shows up as a problem the hero meets and solves. One named historical anecdote per chapter (2003 blackout, 1994 LA Milky Way calls, Siffre 1962, Selkirk, Chernobyl wolves/horses) gives credibility.

Plant and pay off: the dog on the lead (0:16) -> mother of Tins (4:14); the bank billboard (0:12) -> the man you talk to (6:45); the coffee crossroads (0:12) -> birch wood (9:42); the saved peaches tin (3:10) -> opened when the aliens land (10:55). Callbacks reward people who watch to the end and give the ending emotional weight.

Dry, specific jokes as rhythm: 'approved at nobody', 'designed for nobody', 'two small fires', 'so now you have an alarm clock', 'You don't talk about year seven', 'They're 20 years late and they've parked on the cabbages'. Understatement, not gags.
Repeated phrase as a motif: 'for nobody' / 'nobody' (trains, lights, reactors, engineers, the ISS) carries the loneliness theme without saying it.
Upside first, then the turn: 30 s of wish-fulfilment (free pastries, dream car, penthouse) before 'It can't keep that up.' This is the classic what-if bait-and-switch.
An emotional hold after every win (first bulb, Milky Way, cake, CQ): 10-15 s of music with no narration. It makes an explainer feel like a short film.
A rapid montage to cover time: 'Year two, ... Year three, ...', one line, one fact or joke per year, with the same camera angle and a corner year tag, so 8 years fit into 36 s.
Credibility pivot before the twist: 'Everything up to now scientists more or less agree on. This next part, nobody can tell you.' It allows a fiction ending without spending the trust earned so far.
Infographics on plain cream paper with very few elements (a seesaw, a growing timeline, concentric rings, a tally bar), built up in step with the narration. Cheap to make and very clear.
Thumbnail: a before/after split with the same character, two yellow labels, and the time span as the only text.

code_only_remake_requirements.assets: One rigged SVG hero (head, 2 eye states, mouth set, goggles with a removable lens, beard layer at 3 lengths, satchel, 4-5 body poses: from behind, walking, holding, sitting, at a desk), a dog in 3 ages (puppy, adult, grey) with 3 poses, about 12 SVG backgrounds drawn in flat 2.5D perspective (cafe, street with billboard, river skyline, penthouse window, stairwell, supermarket aisle, cottage plus allotments high angle, pharmacy shelf, beach, radio desk, water tower, stadium), an icon set for infographics (power station, city block, reactor, fridge, tins, pills, rice sack, dog silhouettes, calendar, sun, solar panel, radiator, cockroach, horse, Earth), and a split-flap sign component.
code_only_remake_requirements.layout: 16:9 1920x1080. Scenes fill the frame; infographics on a #EEE8DC-ish cream with a soft vignette, thin dark linework, one accent (teal #4FA3A5 or red #C0392B) and a small geometric sans for labels; chapter sign bottom-left over the establishing shot; year tag top-right during montages.
code_only_remake_requirements.camera: Mostly static frames with slow push-ins (scale 1.00 -> 1.05 over 4-6 s), a few lateral trucks across shelves, one long zoom-out (map -> globe), and parallax layers on the skyline shots. Everything can be done with Remotion interpolate() on transform.
code_only_remake_requirements.motion: Infographic elements appear in sync with the narration (opacity plus 6-10 px rise, or draw-on stroke via strokeDashoffset), bars that grow, counters that tick, rings that grow (r interpolation), a seesaw rotation with spring(). Split-flap flips as scaleY on two halves. Steam curls and blinking UI as loops. A light that sweeps out over the city as a staged opacity mask over the window layers.
code_only_remake_requirements.time_lapse_reuse: Make the establishing skyline and the cottage high view as parametric SVG scenes with props for season (palette swap, snow overlay, blossom/leaf colours), decay level (broken windows, vines, overgrowth blobs) and night (dark overlay plus lit windows), so one scene renders every chapter card and the years montage.
code_only_remake_requirements.captions: None in the video (it relies on clean narration); optional for our version.
code_only_remake_requirements.audio: Calm British-English (or neutral) Kokoro/Piper voice at about 160 wpm, second person; a soft piano/ambient bed with 10-15 s music-only holds at emotional beats; small sound effects (card beep, lift ding, tap cough, flap clicks, Morse beeps).
code_only_remake_requirements.effort_note: About 60 shots in 11 minutes. The infographic half is quick to do in code. The character scenes need a reusable pose library and layered SVG sets; low-poly 3D cars and buildings can become flat isometric SVG blocks. A 3-5 minute version with 4 chapter cards would be a realistic first pilot.
